faqs.a: No. An ORRI is independent of who owns the minerals or surface, it's tied strictly to the lease and well it was carved from, and it stays with you regardless of any subsequent sale of the underlying land or minerals.

faqs.q: What happens to your ORRI if the operator re-leases after the current lease expires?
faqs.a: Generally nothing, your override typically does not carry forward into a brand new lease, since it was carved from the original lease specifically, which is why an ORRI's value is closely tied to the current well's remaining life.

faqs.q: How do you confirm the size of your override interest?
faqs.a: The original assignment document, recorded at the county where the well is located, will state your override percentage, and your royalty statement should reflect that same decimal applied to production.

faqs.q: Is an ORRI riskier to hold than a mineral interest?
faqs.a: In one sense yes, since it has a defined end point tied to the lease and well, but that finite structure is simply part of how it should be valued and sold rather than a flaw in the interest itself.

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: Hold a working interest in a North Dakota Bakken well, from a non-op position or old family partnership? Here is what it means and how to sell it.

sections.html:
A cousin of ours ended up holding a small working interest through an old partnership his dad signed onto decades back, and it took him a while to understand why his checks looked so different from ours.

A working interest is fundamentally different from the royalty and mineral interests most North Dakota families hold, it's an operating interest, meaning the owner shares in both the revenue from production and the actual costs of drilling and operating the well. Working interest owners in the Bakken are typically operators themselves, or non-operating partners who took a small stake through a joint operating agreement, an old family drilling partnership, or an assignment from an operator raising capital for a well.

If you're receiving joint interest billing statements alongside, or instead of, a straightforward royalty check, that's the clearest sign you hold a working interest rather than a royalty or mineral interest, and it changes both your obligations and your options considerably.

sections.title: Why a working interest is different from royalty income
sections.html:
A royalty owner never pays a dime toward drilling or operating a well, their share is free of those costs by definition. A working interest owner, by contrast, is billed their proportionate share of drilling costs, workovers, and ongoing lease operating expenses, on top of receiving their proportionate share of revenue. That means a working interest can actually cost you money in a given month if operating expenses outpace production revenue, particularly on an older well needing repair or in a low price environment.

This cost exposure is exactly why working interests carry more risk than royalty interests, and why owners who inherited a small non-operated working interest through an old family partnership sometimes find themselves surprised by a bill rather than a check.

sections.title: Non-operated positions and how they typically arose
sections.html:
Most individual North Dakota working interest owners hold non-operated positions, meaning they don't run day-to-day operations, an operator like the ones active across the Bakken and Three Forks handles that, but they still share proportionately in costs and revenue under a joint operating agreement. These positions frequently trace back to older family drilling partnerships from earlier decades of North Dakota oil activity, or to an operator assigning a small working interest to a landowner as part of an original lease negotiation.

If you're not sure whether your interest is a working interest or a royalty interest, check whether you've ever received a joint interest billing statement, separate from a royalty statement, since that billing is the clearest marker of working interest ownership.

sections.title: Selling a working interest
sections.html:
Working interests are sellable, and doing so relieves you of ongoing cost exposure along with the revenue share, which is often the whole point for an owner who inherited a small non-operated position and would rather not track joint interest billing statements or field calls about workover decisions. Buyers value a working interest against net revenue after typical operating costs, remaining reserves on the well, and any deferred liabilities like plugging obligations that may transfer with the interest.

Because plugging and abandonment liability can attach to a working interest, this is one area where it's worth having a straightforward conversation early about exactly what's transferring and what isn't, so there are no surprises on either side.

sections.title: Reading a joint interest billing statement
sections.html:
A joint interest billing, or JIB, statement lists your proportionate share of specific costs for a given period, drilling, completion, workovers, or routine operating expenses, alongside your proportionate share of revenue for the same period, netted against each other. Unlike a royalty statement, which is almost purely revenue, a JIB can show a net amount owed to you or a net amount you owe, depending on how the month's activity and expenses shook out.

If a JIB statement looks unfamiliar or the math doesn't add up against what you expected, the operator's accounting department can usually walk through the specific charges, and it's worth asking rather than assuming an unusual bill is simply how things work.

faqs.q: Why did you get a bill instead of a check this month?
faqs.a: That's typical for a working interest when operating or drilling costs for the period exceeded your share of production revenue, since working interest owners share proportionately in both costs and revenue, unlike royalty owners.

faqs.q: Is a working interest riskier than owning minerals or a royalty?
faqs.a: Generally yes, because you're exposed to operating costs and potential liability, including plugging obligations, in addition to the same commodity price and production risk every interest type carries.

faqs.q: Can you sell a working interest that currently owes more than it earns?
faqs.a: It can be more difficult, since a buyer has to weigh the cost exposure and any liabilities against future revenue, but it's not impossible, and a straightforward conversation about the well's specific numbers is the place to start.

faqs.q: Does selling a working interest end your exposure to future plugging costs?
faqs.a: Generally the buyer assumes that liability going forward as part of taking on the interest, though the specific terms of the assignment should spell this out clearly before you sign anything.

items.name: Bakken Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own minerals under the Bakken or Three Forks in North Dakota? Here is how the play actually pays, what your statement means, and how to get an offer.

sections.html:
A western North Dakota owner ran cattle over ground that turned out to be sitting on the Bakken, and by the time your dad was managing the checkbook, half the review desk's neighbors could recite formation names like scripture.

The Bakken is a shale formation stacked between older marine rock, and it runs under most of the Williston Basin in western North Dakota, eastern Montana, and up into Saskatchewan. Below it sits the Three Forks, a second productive zone that operators now drill almost as often as the Bakken itself. If your family's minerals sit in McKenzie, Mountrail, Dunn, Williams, Burke, Divide, or McLean County, there is a real chance both zones have been tested, leased, or drilled under your acreage at some point since the horizontal boom took off in the mid-2000s.

The North Dakota review specialists sold the review desk's own minerals out of a family trust a decade back, after years of watching a royalty check swing with oil prices and rail differentials neither of the review desk controlled. What the North Dakota review specialists learned then still holds: understanding the play matters more than any single number on an offer letter.

sections.title: How the Bakken and Three Forks actually produce
sections.html:
Operators drill horizontal wells two miles or more into the Bakken's middle dolomitic layer, or into one of several benches within the Three Forks, then hydraulically fracture the wellbore in dozens of stages. A single well often drains a large modern spacing unit, which is why the North Dakota Industrial Commission has pushed many units toward 1,280 acres instead of the older 640-acre standard. If your tract is inside one of these larger units, your fractional share of production may have changed even if nothing was ever drilled on your specific quarter section.

Production from a horizontal Bakken well behaves nothing like a vertical well from the old days. Initial rates can be strong, but decline in the first year is steep, often 60 percent or more, before settling into a long, shallow tail that can run for decades. That curve is exactly why a royalty check from year one looks so different from a check on the same well five years later, and why buyers price minerals against a blend of near-term cash flow and long-tail expectation rather than a single month's statement.

sections.title: Reading a Bakken royalty statement
sections.html:
Companies like Continental Resources, Hess, Marathon, Whiting, Oasis, and Slawson historically operated large positions across the play, and each issues statements with its own layout, but the mechanics are similar. Look for the gross production volume, the price received (Bakken crude has often sold at a discount to West Texas Intermediate because of pipeline and rail logistics out of the basin), post-production deductions for gathering and processing, and your net decimal interest applied at the bottom.

Gas royalty lines confuse a lot of owners, because associated gas in the Bakken has sometimes been flared or vented rather than sold, especially on newer wells waiting for gas capture infrastructure. If your statement shows oil revenue but little or no gas revenue on an active well, that is often the reason, not an error in your interest calculation.

sections.title: What buyers weigh when they price Bakken minerals
sections.html:
A buyer will typically want your net mineral acreage, your decimal interest under the producing unit, recent statements showing actual volumes and price received, and whatever lease terms are on file at the county recorder. Undeveloped acreage in the core of the play, where operators have been active with multiple wells per section, tends to draw more interest than flank acreage where only a single well has been drilled or where the lease has expired without a well.

Value talk should always be hedged against current activity rather than stated as a flat number, since Bakken pricing moves with oil markets, differential spreads, and how close an operator's next pad is to your unit. Anyone quoting you a guaranteed figure before reviewing your actual decimal interest and recent statements is skipping the part of the work that matters.

faqs.q: Does the Bakken or the Three Forks pay differently?
faqs.a: Both zones are priced against the same oil and gas markets, so the difference usually comes down to which bench was drilled, how many wells target your specific spacing unit, and where your tract sits relative to the operator's development plan, not the formation name itself.

faqs.q: Your statement shows a big drop from last year. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Often yes. Bakken wells decline quickly in year one and two, so a statement two or three years after first production can look much smaller than an early check, even with no change in your ownership or the price of oil.

faqs.q: What counties are considered the core of the Bakken in North Dakota?
faqs.a: McKenzie, Mountrail, and Dunn County have historically seen the heaviest horizontal drilling density, with Williams, Burke, Divide, and McLean County holding strong but somewhat lighter activity depending on the specific township.

faqs.q: Do you need to know your exact decimal interest before you get an offer?
faqs.a: No. A recent division order or royalty statement is enough to get started, and the North Dakota review specialists can help you interpret it against county records if you are not sure what your fractional interest actually is.

faqs.q: Can undeveloped Bakken acreage still be worth selling?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly in the core counties where an operator holds an active lease or has drilled nearby units, though pricing on undeveloped ground depends heavily on how close and how recent that activity is.

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A step-by-step look at selling North Dakota mineral rights, from figuring out what you own to closing, written by a family that's done it.

sections.html:
Selling mineral rights in North Dakota isn't complicated once you know the order of operations, but almost nobody explains that order before you're already three offers deep.

The North Dakota review specialists are a fourth-generation ranch family out of the western part of the state, and the North Dakota review specialists sold a piece of the review desk's own mineral interest years before the North Dakota review specialists ever bought anyone else's. That's part of why the North Dakota review specialists do this the way the North Dakota review specialists do. The North Dakota review specialists know what it feels like to get a letter offering to buy something you inherited and not fully understand what you're holding. This guide walks through the actual steps, in the order they happen, without the sales pitch.

sections.title: Step one: figure out exactly what you own
sections.html:
Before you can sell anything, you need to know your net mineral acres, which county they're in, and whether they're currently leased or producing. If you have a recent property tax statement for the minerals, a lease, or a royalty check stub, that's your starting point. If you're not sure, a buyer can usually help you pull the county records once you tell them the legal description or the name on the original deed.

It also matters whether you're selling all your minerals or just a portion, and whether you want to sell the royalty interest under an existing lease versus the minerals themselves. Those are different transactions with different tax treatment, and it's worth understanding the difference before you're comparing offers.

sections.title: Step two: get more than one look at value
sections.html:
Mineral value in North Dakota depends heavily on where your acreage sits relative to the Bakken and Three Forks producing trend, whether it's already leased or producing, and what nearby wells have been doing. A tract in the core of McKenzie or Mountrail County with an active well on it is a different animal than undeveloped acreage on the fringe of the play, and any honest buyer will tell you that rather than quoting one flat number for the whole state.

It's reasonable to talk to more than one buyer. Offers can vary depending on how a buyer values production history, decline curves, and future drilling potential, so getting a second opinion costs you nothing but a phone call.

sections.title: Step three: review the offer and the paperwork
sections.html:
A real offer should spell out the net mineral acres being purchased, the county and legal description, the price, and whether it includes any existing lease or excludes a reserved royalty. Read it slowly. Ask what happens to any royalty payments already in process, and confirm the closing timeline in writing.

This is also the point to loop in your attorney or CPA if the sale is large, if the ownership is shared among heirs, or if you're unsure how the proceeds will be taxed. It's a short conversation that heads off a lot of second-guessing later.

sections.title: Step four: closing
sections.html:
Closing on a mineral sale usually means signing a mineral deed, which the buyer then records at the county courthouse in the county where the minerals sit. Funds are typically wired or sent by check once the deed is executed and any title questions are resolved. A clean sale with straightforward title can close in a matter of weeks. One with heirship issues or a title gap takes longer, but that's normal for family land that's passed through a few generations without every step being formally recorded.

After closing, you're done. No more decisions about future leases, no more waiting on a well's decline curve, no more mail from operators you've never heard of. For some families that's the whole point.

The North Dakota review specialists have heard from more than a few owners who describe the closing call as the first time in years they didn't have to think about a well in a county they'd never visited. That relief is real, even if the acreage itself never meant much to them beyond a line on a tax statement.

faqs.q: How long does selling mineral rights in North Dakota usually take?
faqs.a: A straightforward sale with clear title can close in two to four weeks. Sales involving multiple heirs, unprobated estates, or unclear legal descriptions take longer while that paperwork gets sorted out.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell all your minerals at once?
faqs.a: No, many owners sell only a portion of their acreage or a percentage of their interest, keeping the rest. This is worth discussing directly with a buyer if you want to retain part of your ownership.

faqs.q: What if your minerals aren't currently leased or producing?
faqs.a: You can still sell undeveloped or unleased minerals, though the offer will reflect that there's no current production history to point to, and value typically depends more on the acreage's position relative to active drilling nearby.

faqs.q: Will selling affect your taxes?
faqs.a: Selling mineral rights is generally a taxable event, often treated differently than ordinary royalty income. Talk to your CPA or attorney about your specific situation before closing.

faqs.q: Can you sell if the interest came through inheritance and was never probated?
faqs.a: Often yes, though it may require a small estate affidavit or a short probate first. A buyer who has done this before should be able to walk you through what North Dakota requires for your situation.

faqs.q: What if you only recently found out you own minerals?
faqs.a: This happens more than you'd think, especially with acreage passed down through a great-grandparent's homestead. Start by finding the county where the land sits, and a title search from there can usually confirm what you actually hold.

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: A grounded look at what drives North Dakota mineral rights value: production, location in the play, decline curves, and current oil prices.

sections.html:
Value is the question every mineral owner in North Dakota eventually asks, and the honest answer is that it depends on a handful of specific things about your acreage, not one number that applies statewide.

The North Dakota review specialists get asked what minerals are worth almost every week, usually from someone who inherited an interest and has no idea where to start. The North Dakota review specialists have sold the review desk's own, so the North Dakota review specialists understand the instinct to want a quick number. But quoting one flat figure for the whole state would be doing exactly what the North Dakota review specialists tell people to watch out for from other buyers. Value depends on where your acreage sits and what's actually happening on it.

sections.title: Location within the Bakken and Three Forks matters most
sections.html:
North Dakota's mineral value is tied heavily to the Bakken and Three Forks formations, and not all acreage sits in the same position relative to that play. Core counties like McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, and Dunn have seen the heaviest, most consistent drilling activity for over a decade, while acreage on the fringes of the play, or in counties with less consistent drilling history, generally carries more uncertainty.

This is why two owners with the same acreage size can hear very different numbers from a buyer, depending entirely on which county, and often which specific spacing unit, their minerals sit in.

sections.title: Whether you're leased, unleased, or producing
sections.html:
Producing minerals with an active well and real royalty history give a buyer something concrete to project future income from. Leased but not yet producing acreage carries more uncertainty, since it depends on when or whether the operator drills. Unleased, undeveloped minerals carry the most uncertainty of all, since there's no lease bonus history or production data to point to.

In general, production history is what turns a rough estimate into a firmer number, which is part of why the North Dakota review specialists always ask for recent royalty statements or division orders as a starting point.

sections.title: Decline curves and well age
sections.html:
Bakken and Three Forks wells typically produce heavily in their first couple of years, then decline steadily after that. A well two years into production is worth valuing very differently than one that's been in decline for eight or ten years, even if both are producing on similar-sized units. Buyers factor remaining productive life into their valuation, which is part of why offers on the same acreage can shift over time as the well ages.

Newer wells drilled with modern completion techniques have also generally produced more per lateral foot than older vertical wells, which is another reason vintage matters as much as location.

sections.title: Oil prices and market conditions
sections.html:
Because royalty income moves directly with oil and gas prices, mineral values tend to track market conditions over time, rising when prices are strong and softening when they pull back. This is one reason offers you get today may look different from offers a year ago or a year from now, and it's part of why the North Dakota review specialists talk in ranges tied to current activity rather than fixed numbers.

If you're comparing offers, it's fair to ask a buyer how recent oil prices and nearby well performance factored into their number, rather than accepting a flat figure without explanation.

The North Dakota review specialists have seen offers on the same acreage shift by a meaningful margin over the course of a single year purely because of price swings, with nothing else about the underlying wells changing at all. That's not a sign anyone did anything wrong, it's just how closely tied mineral value is to the commodity itself.

faqs.q: Is there a per-acre price you can use to estimate your minerals?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Value varies too much by county, spacing unit, well age, and current market conditions for a single per-acre figure to mean much without looking at your specific acreage.

faqs.q: Are minerals in McKenzie County worth more than other counties?
faqs.a: McKenzie County has historically seen some of the heaviest drilling activity in the Bakken, but value still depends on the specific spacing unit and production history, not the county name alone.

faqs.q: Does an older, declining well mean your minerals are worth less?
faqs.a: Typically yes, since less future production remains to be projected, though older wells can still hold value, especially if there's potential for future infill drilling on the same unit.

faqs.q: How often Should you get your minerals re-evaluated?
faqs.a: There's no fixed schedule, but it's reasonable to check in whenever nearby drilling activity picks up, a new well is permitted on your unit, or oil prices shift significantly.

faqs.q: Can you get a rough sense of value without selling?
faqs.a: Yes, a real buyer should be willing to walk through the factors driving value on your specific acreage even if you're just exploring the idea and not ready to commit.

faqs.q: Does the number of wells on your unit affect value?
faqs.a: Yes, spacing units with multiple producing wells generally show a fuller production picture than a unit with just one well, though each well's individual age and decline still matters more than the raw count.

items.name: Reading Your Royalty Statements
items.meta: A line-by-line guide to reading North Dakota royalty statements, including multi-well Bakken statements and the deductions taken out of your check.

sections.html:
A North Dakota royalty statement can run several pages of tiny numbers when you own interests across multiple wells, and most owners have never had anyone walk them through what it actually says.

The first multi-well statement you ever tried to read looked like a spreadsheet someone forgot to format for humans. Rows and rows of well names, decimal interests, deduction codes, all crammed onto legal-size paper. It took you an evening with your dad and a calculator to understand it wasn't complicated, it was just dense. Once you know what each column means, it reads a lot faster.

sections.title: The basics: what each line represents
sections.html:
Every royalty statement repeats a few core pieces of information for each well: the well name and API number, your decimal interest in that well, the product sold (oil, gas, or natural gas liquids), the volume produced attributable to your interest, the price received, and the deductions taken before your net check amount. If you own interests in several wells, a multi-well statement simply repeats this block for each one, then totals everything at the bottom.

Your decimal interest should match what's on your division order for that well. If it doesn't, that's the first thing to flag with the operator's owner relations department, since a mismatched decimal is one of the more common statement errors.

sections.title: Reading a multi-well Bakken statement
sections.html:
Because so many North Dakota mineral owners hold fractional interests across large spacing units, it's common to see royalty income coming from several wells on the same unit, sometimes six or eight wells drilled in phases over a few years. Each well will show its own volume and price, since wells brought online at different times will be at different points on their decline curve, some near peak production and others well into decline.

Don't be surprised if the total check amount shifts noticeably month to month, even without anything going wrong. Oil and gas prices move, a well might be shut in temporarily for maintenance or offset drilling nearby, and production naturally declines over time. Look at trends over several months rather than reacting to any single statement.

sections.title: Understanding deductions
sections.html:
Most North Dakota royalty statements include deductions for post-production costs, things like gathering, transportation, processing, and compression, taken out before you're paid, depending on your specific lease language. Some older leases have language limiting or prohibiting certain deductions, which is part of why keeping a copy of your original lease matters even years after signing it.

Common deduction codes include GTH for gathering, TRANS for transportation, PROC for processing, and COMP for compression, though exact labels vary by operator. If deductions on your statement seem unusually high relative to the gross value, or if they've increased notably without explanation, it's worth a direct call to the operator asking them to itemize it.

sections.title: Checking your statement against what you expect
sections.html:
Compare production volumes and prices to nearby wells if you can find that data through the North Dakota Industrial Commission's public records, which track monthly production by well. This won't tell you exactly what you should be paid, since deductions and pricing arrangements vary, but it gives you a reasonable sanity check against wild swings that don't match what the field is actually doing.

If you're weighing whether to keep collecting royalty income long term or sell your interest outright, your statements are also the best evidence of real production history, and a serious buyer will always want to see them before making a firm offer.

It's worth setting aside a folder, physical or digital, just for these statements, sorted by well, so you can pull up several months of history in one place instead of digging through a stack of mail every time a question comes up.

faqs.q: Why does your royalty check change every month?
faqs.a: Oil and gas prices fluctuate, well production naturally declines over time, and wells are occasionally shut in for maintenance or nearby drilling, all of which cause month-to-month variation that's normal rather than a sign of a mistake.

faqs.q: What are post-production deductions?
faqs.a: These are costs for gathering, transporting, processing, and compressing the oil or gas after it leaves the wellhead, which some leases allow the operator to deduct from your royalty before paying you.

faqs.q: How do you know if your decimal interest is correct?
faqs.a: Compare it to the decimal shown on your original division order for that well. If they don't match, or if you never received a division order for a well appearing on your statement, contact the operator's owner relations department.

faqs.q: Can you dispute deductions you think are too high?
faqs.a: Yes, you can request an itemized breakdown from the operator and compare it against your lease language, which may limit certain deductions depending on how it was originally negotiated.

faqs.q: Should you keep old royalty statements?
faqs.a: Yes, keep them filed by well name for at least several years. They're useful for tax records, for spotting errors over time, and for supporting any future sale of your minerals.

faqs.q: What does it mean if a well on your statement suddenly shows zero production?
faqs.a: This can happen for legitimate reasons, including temporary shut-ins for maintenance, offset well fracturing nearby, or seasonal restrictions, but if it persists for several months without explanation, it's worth calling the operator to ask directly.

items.name: Division Orders Explained
items.meta: A plain-language walkthrough of North Dakota division orders: what the decimal means, why it changes, and what to check before you sign one.

sections.html:
The first division order that lands in a North Dakota mailbox usually raises more questions than it answers, and that's fine, because it's a legal form dressed up as paperwork.

A western North Dakota owner used to say the division order was the only mail he got that took longer to understand than a weather forecast. He wasn't wrong. It's a short form with a long tail, and if you sign it wrong, or sign it without checking it, you can spend years correcting the mistake. The review desk's process reflects real title, division-order, and royalty-statement work from a McKenzie County family mineral file.

sections.title: What a division order actually is
sections.html:
A division order is the operator's statement of who owns what share of production from a well, expressed as a decimal interest, and a request for you to confirm it before they start paying you. It is not the lease. It does not change your ownership. It's an accounting document that tells the operator's revenue department how to split the check among everyone with an interest in that spacing unit.

In North Dakota, most wells are drilled on 1,280-acre units under Bakken and Three Forks spacing orders, so a single division order might be carving your interest down to eight or ten decimal places. That's normal. What matters is whether the decimal matches the acreage and interest type you actually own, not whether the number looks small on the page.

sections.title: Where the decimal comes from
sections.html:
The operator's land department builds your decimal from the county records: your deed, any probate or heirship affidavits, the lease, and the spacing order for that unit. If you own 40 net mineral acres in a 1,280-acre unit under a lease with a standard royalty, the math is your net acres divided by the unit size, times your royalty fraction. Simple in theory. In practice, North Dakota mineral ownership is often split across generations through wills that were never formally probated, and that's where the decimal gets it wrong.

The North Dakota review specialists have seen division orders that undercount an owner's share because the title work only found half the heirs, or because an old deed reserved minerals in a way the land department's title runner read differently than the family understood it. Neither side is necessarily at fault. It's just old paper and small print.

sections.title: Checking it before you sign
sections.html:
Compare the decimal interest on the division order to your own math, or to the interest shown on your last check stub if you've owned this interest a while. Confirm the well name, API number, and county match what you expect. Look at whether it lists you as a working interest owner or a royalty owner, because those are taxed and treated very differently, and a clerical mix-up here is more common than people assume.

If the numbers don't match, you're not stuck. Call the operator's division order department, tell them what you think your correct interest is, and ask what documentation they need. Sometimes it's a copy of a deed. Sometimes it's a certified heirship affidavit. It can take a few letters back and forth, but it beats getting underpaid for years because a form went out with a typo baked into it.

sections.title: What happens after you sign
sections.html:
Once you return a signed division order, the operator starts or corrects your payments based on that decimal. Most operators in North Dakota will pay back to first production or to when your interest became effective, so a delay in signing doesn't usually cost you money, it just delays when the checks start showing up. Keep a copy of every division order you sign, filed by well name, because you'll want it later when a royalty statement doesn't seem to add up.

If you're in the middle of selling your minerals, buyers will want to see your division orders too. They tell a buyer exactly what decimal interest they'd be stepping into, which speeds up an offer instead of leaving it as a guess based on the county plat alone.

faqs.q: Do you have to sign a division order to get paid?
faqs.a: Most operators won't start regular payments until they have a signed division order on file, though North Dakota law generally requires payment of proceeds within a set time after production regardless. Read it carefully rather than signing on the day it arrives, but don't sit on it indefinitely either.

faqs.q: Can a division order change your ownership?
faqs.a: No. It's an accounting confirmation, not a conveyance. Your actual title comes from your deed, will, or heirship documents. If the division order decimal is wrong, it's the paperwork that's wrong, not your underlying ownership.

faqs.q: What if you inherited your interest and never got a division order?
faqs.a: You'll typically need to send the operator a certified copy of the death certificate, the will or a court order determining heirs, and sometimes an affidavit of heirship, before they'll issue a new division order in your name.

faqs.q: Why does your decimal interest have so many digits?
faqs.a: North Dakota's large spacing units, often 1,280 or 2,560 acres, mean even a full 40-acre mineral tract is a small fraction of the unit, and that fraction gets divided further by your royalty percentage, which produces a long decimal that's normal, not a red flag.

faqs.q: Should you talk to anyone before signing?
faqs.a: If the interest is large, contested among heirs, or the numbers don't match your own records, it's worth a call to your attorney or CPA before you sign, especially if the division order affects how income gets reported for tax purposes.

items.name: Documents You Need to Sell
items.meta: The paperwork a North Dakota mineral sale actually needs, from deeds and division orders to heirship affidavits for family land.

sections.html:
Before anyone can write a real offer on your North Dakota minerals, they need to see paper, and knowing what to gather ahead of time saves weeks off the process.

When the North Dakota review specialists sold a piece of the review desk's own family's minerals a few years back, the slowest part wasn't the negotiating, it was hunting down paperwork that had been stuffed in three different drawers across two houses. Some of it was in your late aunt's handwriting from a 1970s lease renewal. Some of it the North Dakota review specialists had to drive to the courthouse in Watford City to get copies of ourselves. If you gather the right documents up front, a buyer can move fast. If you don't, the whole thing stalls waiting on paper that should have taken a phone call to find.

sections.title: The core ownership documents
sections.html:
Start with your deed, the document that shows how you came to own the minerals, whether that's a mineral deed, a warranty deed with a mineral reservation, or a court order from probate. If you inherited the interest, you'll also need whatever proved that transfer: a will, a decree of distribution, or an affidavit of heirship recorded in the county where the minerals sit.

If your name has changed since the deed was recorded, through marriage or otherwise, bring documentation of that too, because a buyer's title company will flag any mismatch between the name on the deed and the name on the offer.

sections.title: Lease and production paperwork
sections.html:
If your minerals are currently leased, gather a copy of the lease itself, including any amendments or extensions. This tells a buyer the royalty rate, the primary term, and whether the lease is held by production, which matters a great deal in valuing an interest.

If a well is already producing on your acreage, pull together your most recent division orders and a handful of recent royalty check stubs or statements. These show real production history rather than an estimate, and in the review desk's experience they're what turns a rough offer into a firm one.

sections.title: Family and heirship paperwork
sections.html:
A lot of North Dakota mineral ownership traces back through several generations of ranch and farm families, and it's common for an interest to be split among siblings or cousins who each own a fraction. If that's your situation, gather whatever family paperwork exists showing who the current owners are, even if it's informal, because it gives everyone a starting point rather than reconstructing it from scratch.

If part of the ownership was never formally probated, a real buyer will tell you that up front instead of pretending it's not an issue. Sometimes a small estate affidavit is enough. Sometimes it needs a short probate. Either way, knowing this early keeps the timeline honest.

sections.title: What you don't need to track down yourself
sections.html:
You don't need a formal appraisal, a survey, or a title opinion before you talk to a buyer. Those are things a serious buyer runs on their own dime once you're close to a deal, and asking a family to pay for that work up front is backwards. Your job at this stage is just to hand over what you already have, even if it's incomplete.

It's also fine to talk to your CPA or attorney before signing anything, especially if the ownership involves multiple heirs or an estate that hasn't been settled. A short conversation there can save a longer one later.

Even a partial set of paperwork is a fine starting point. If all you have is a tax statement showing the legal description and the county, that's often enough for a buyer to pull the rest of the chain of title from public records and figure out what's missing.

faqs.q: What if you can't find your original deed?
faqs.a: The county recorder's office in the county where your minerals sit keeps recorded copies going back decades. A quick call or visit, sometimes even a search on the county's own online index, will usually turn up a copy for a small fee.

faqs.q: Do you need a title company before you get an offer?
faqs.a: No. Title work happens after you've agreed to terms, as part of closing. A buyer shouldn't ask a family to pay for title work just to receive an offer.

faqs.q: Your interest was never formally probated, Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Often yes, though it may require a small estate affidavit or a short probate first depending on North Dakota law and the size of the estate. This is worth a conversation with an attorney early rather than late.

faqs.q: What if multiple family members own the same interest?
faqs.a: Each owner generally needs to sign their own deed to convey their share, though co-owners can often move through the process together once everyone agrees on terms.

faqs.q: What if a western North Dakota family's paperwork is scattered across different relatives?
faqs.a: That's common with ranch families where documents got split up between siblings or passed down piecemeal. Gather what you can from each branch of the family and share it as you find it, rather than waiting until you have everything in one place before reaching out.

faqs.q: Do you need copies of every royalty check you have ever received?
faqs.a: No, a handful of recent statements is usually enough to show current production, along with your division order for that well.

items.name: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
items.meta: Warning signs of a lowball mineral rights offer in North Dakota, from vague per-acre numbers to pressure tactics, and what a fair offer looks like.

sections.html:
North Dakota mineral owners get letters from buyers they've never heard of every year, and some of those offers are fair while others are counting on you never checking the math.

The North Dakota review specialists have received the review desk's share of unsolicited letters over the years about minerals the review desk's own family owns, some offering numbers so low they weren't worth a phone call back. It taught the review desk what to look for, and it's part of why the North Dakota review specialists explain the review desk's own offers the way the North Dakota review specialists do now. A lowball offer isn't always dishonest on its face, sometimes it's just lazy, built on a form letter sent to every mineral owner in a county without looking at what's actually happening on that specific acreage.

sections.title: Vague per-acre numbers with no explanation
sections.html:
Be cautious of any letter that quotes a flat dollar figure per acre with no mention of your specific well, spacing unit, or production history. Real value in North Dakota depends on where your acreage sits relative to the Bakken and Three Forks trend and what's actually producing on your unit, so a number that ignores that entirely is usually a starting point designed to be low, not a considered offer.

A fair buyer should be able to explain why they landed on their number, referencing your county, your unit's production if it has any, and recent nearby activity, rather than reciting a figure that could apply to any parcel in the state.

sections.title: Pressure to sign quickly
sections.html:
Watch for language pushing you to sign within days, or offers that claim to expire almost immediately. Mineral sales are not typically time-sensitive in a way that requires a rushed decision, and a buyer leaning on urgency is often trying to keep you from comparing offers or asking questions.

It's reasonable to take a week or more to review paperwork, talk to family co-owners, or run the offer past your attorney or CPA. A legitimate buyer won't disappear over that.

sections.title: Offers that ignore existing production
sections.html:
If you already have a producing well on your acreage with real royalty history, and an offer doesn't ask to see your division orders or recent statements before quoting a number, that's a sign the offer wasn't built on your actual production. Production history is usually the strongest evidence of value a mineral owner has, and any buyer skipping it is either guessing or hoping you won't notice.

Similarly, be wary of an offer letter listing the wrong well, wrong county, or an acreage figure that doesn't match your own records. It suggests the letter was generated in bulk rather than researched specifically for your ownership.

sections.title: What a fair offer actually looks like
sections.html:
A fair offer references your specific county and, where relevant, the wells producing on your unit. It explains, even briefly, how the number was reached, and it gives you time to review it, ask questions, and compare it against another buyer if you'd like. It also avoids words like guaranteed or highest-paying, because no honest buyer can promise a specific outcome before reviewing your actual title and production.

If something about an offer feels off, trust that instinct and ask more questions before signing anything. A good offer holds up to scrutiny.

The North Dakota review specialists have had families forward the review desk offer letters they received from other buyers just to ask whether the number sounded reasonable, and the North Dakota review specialists are always glad to give an honest read on it, even when it means telling them the number looked fair and there was nothing to worry about. That kind of second opinion costs nothing and often settles the question in a single phone call.

faqs.q: Is a low first offer always a lowball offer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, some buyers start conservative and adjust once they review your division orders and production history. The key is whether they're willing to explain their reasoning and reconsider based on real documentation.

faqs.q: Should you get more than one offer before deciding?
faqs.a: Yes, comparing offers from more than one buyer is a normal and reasonable step, and it costs you nothing but time.

faqs.q: What if a buyer won't explain how they reached their number?
faqs.a: That's worth treating as a caution flag. A buyer confident in their offer should be willing to walk through the factors behind it, including your county, well production, and current market conditions.

faqs.q: Can you negotiate a mineral rights offer?
faqs.a: Yes, offers are typically a starting point for discussion, not a final take-it-or-leave-it number, especially once you've provided additional documentation like division orders or recent statements.

faqs.q: Is it worth talking to an attorney before accepting any offer?
faqs.a: For larger interests, contested ownership, or anything that feels unclear, yes, a short conversation with your attorney or CPA before signing is worth the time.

faqs.q: What if a buyer's letter uses aggressive or urgent language?
faqs.a: Treat that as a signal to slow down rather than speed up. Phrases pushing you toward an immediate decision are more about closing the deal on the buyer's terms than giving you a fair shot at understanding your acreage.

items.name: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer
items.meta: How mineral deeds and title transfer actually work in North Dakota, from recording at the courthouse to fixing old title gaps in family land.

sections.html:
A mineral deed looks like a short, plain document, but it's the piece of paper that actually moves ownership, and getting it right matters more than any other form in the process.

A western North Dakota family has recorded deeds at the McKenzie County courthouse for four generations now, some going back to homestead-era transfers, and the North Dakota review specialists have learned that the deed itself is usually the simple part. It's the chain leading up to it, who owned it before, how it passed through wills or was never formally settled, that takes the real time. This is a plain look at how mineral deeds and title transfer work in North Dakota.

sections.title: What a mineral deed does
sections.html:
A mineral deed conveys ownership of the minerals themselves, separate from the surface, from one party to another. It includes the legal description of the land, the county, the grantor and grantee, and typically the net mineral acres being conveyed. Once signed and recorded at the county recorder's office, it becomes the public record of who owns that interest.

In North Dakota, mineral ownership was severed from surface ownership on a lot of ranch and farm land generations ago, sometimes when the land was originally homesteaded, sometimes later when a family sold the surface but kept the minerals. That severance is why you can own minerals under land you've never set foot on, and why title tracing sometimes means going back to records from the early twentieth century.

sections.title: Recording and why it matters
sections.html:
A deed is signed, then it's recorded with the county recorder in the county where the minerals are located, which puts the transfer on public record and protects the new owner's claim against later disputes. Recording fees are modest, but the step itself is what makes a transfer enforceable against third parties, so it's not something to skip or delay.

If you're buying or selling, always confirm the deed gets recorded and get a copy of the recorded version, with the county's stamp and instrument number on it, for your own files.

sections.title: Common title gaps in family-owned minerals
sections.html:
The most common issue the North Dakota review specialists see with ranch family mineral interests is an estate that was never formally probated. A grandparent passes minerals informally to their children, everyone knows who owns what within the family, but nothing was ever filed at the courthouse. Decades later, when it's time to sell or lease, the title doesn't show clear ownership, even though everyone in the family agrees on the facts.

This is fixable, usually with an affidavit of heirship, a small estate proceeding, or in more complicated cases a short probate, but it takes time to put together the right documents. It's worth starting this process early if you know your family's title has a gap, rather than waiting until you're trying to close a sale under a deadline.

sections.title: What a clean transfer looks like
sections.html:
A clean transfer starts with a title search confirming the current owner of record, followed by a properly executed deed with an accurate legal description, signed and notarized, then recorded at the correct county. If minerals are being sold, the buyer typically handles recording as part of closing, though it's smart to confirm this rather than assume it.

If your family's title has any wrinkles, an unprobated estate, a name change, a deed with an unclear legal description, it's worth talking to your attorney before you're mid-transaction. Fixing a title issue calmly, ahead of time, is a lot easier than fixing it while a closing date is bearing down.

The North Dakota review specialists have walked several families through exactly this kind of cleanup on their own home place, and it's rarely as complicated as it first appears once someone sits down and traces the chain of title step by step.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to transfer mineral rights?
faqs.a: It's not always required, but it's wise, especially if the deed's legal description is complex, if multiple heirs are involved, or if there's any question about the current chain of title.

faqs.q: What happens if a deed is never recorded?
faqs.a: An unrecorded deed can still be valid between the original parties, but it leaves the transfer off the public record, which can create disputes later and typically prevents a subsequent buyer or lender from relying on it.

faqs.q: Can you transfer minerals to your children now instead of through a will?
faqs.a: Yes, minerals can be conveyed by deed at any time, including gifting them to heirs during your lifetime, though there are tax and estate planning considerations worth discussing with your CPA or attorney first.

faqs.q: What if the legal description on the old deed doesn't match current county records?
faqs.a: This happens more often than people expect on older ranch land. A title company or attorney can usually reconcile the description, sometimes requiring a corrective deed to fix it.

faqs.q: How long does it take to record a deed in North Dakota?
faqs.a: Recording itself is usually quick once the deed is properly executed, often just days, but resolving any underlying title issues beforehand can take considerably longer depending on their complexity.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a mineral deed and a royalty deed?
faqs.a: A mineral deed conveys ownership of the minerals themselves, including the right to lease them, while a royalty deed conveys only the right to receive royalty payments from production, without the leasing rights that come with the minerals.

items.name: Lease vs. Sell: Which Is Right?
items.meta: Weighing whether to lease or sell your North Dakota mineral rights, with the real tradeoffs between ongoing royalty income and a lump sum.

sections.html:
Leasing and selling solve two different problems, and the right answer usually comes down to what you actually want the money for and how much uncertainty you're willing to carry.

The North Dakota review specialists have done both. A western North Dakota family has signed leases on ground that's still producing today, and the North Dakota review specialists have sold other interests outright when it made more sense than waiting on a well that might never get drilled. Neither choice is automatically better. It depends on your acreage, your age, your family situation, and honestly, how much you want to keep thinking about oil and gas paperwork every quarter.

sections.title: What leasing actually gives you
sections.html:
Leasing means you keep ownership of the minerals and grant an operator the right to drill, in exchange for a bonus payment up front and a royalty on future production, typically somewhere between an eighth and a fifth of the value produced, depending on the lease terms negotiated at the time. If a well gets drilled and produces well, a lease can pay out for years, sometimes decades, especially with newer horizontal wells in the Bakken and Three Forks that can hold production for a long stretch before steep decline sets in.

The tradeoff is that leasing keeps you exposed to everything that comes with owning minerals long term: fluctuating oil prices, well decline, the operator's own priorities about when or whether to drill at all, and the paperwork of tracking royalty statements for as long as you hold the interest.

sections.title: What selling actually gives you
sections.html:
Selling converts your mineral interest into a lump sum today, all at once, and you're done. No more royalty statements to check, no more wondering whether the operator will drill your unit next year or in ten years, no more worrying about what happens to your interest if you pass it to heirs who live out of state and don't want to deal with North Dakota mineral paperwork.

The tradeoff is that you give up any future upside. If new wells get drilled on your acreage after you sell, or if oil prices climb and production value rises with them, that benefit goes to whoever bought your interest, not to you.

sections.title: Questions that usually point to an answer
sections.html:
Ask yourself whether you need the money now for something specific, like paying down debt, funding retirement, or settling an estate among several heirs who'd rather split cash than co-own a fractional mineral interest across state lines. If yes, selling often makes more sense. Ask whether you're comfortable with years of unpredictable royalty income that depends on oil prices and a well's decline curve. If that unpredictability doesn't bother you and you don't need the cash, leasing and holding might suit you better.

It also matters whether your acreage is in the core of the play or on the edge of it. Interests near active, productive wells in counties like McKenzie, Mountrail, or Williams tend to draw stronger interest from both lessees and buyers, while acreage farther from current drilling activity may see less certainty either way.

sections.title: You don't have to choose only one
sections.html:
Some owners split the decision, selling a portion of their minerals for immediate cash while keeping the rest to lease and hold for potential future royalty income. That can be a reasonable middle path if you want some certainty now without giving up every bit of long-term upside.

There's no wrong answer here, only the one that fits your family's situation. If the decision touches an estate with multiple heirs or has real tax consequences, it's worth a conversation with your attorney or CPA before you commit either way.

The review desk's own family chose to sell part of an interest and keep another piece leased, mostly because the portion the North Dakota review specialists sold had been split so many ways among cousins that managing it jointly had become more trouble than it was worth, while the piece the North Dakota review specialists kept was still close enough to home that the North Dakota review specialists didn't mind holding onto it.

faqs.q: Is selling always worth less than leasing over time?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. It depends on future drilling, oil prices, and how long a well continues producing at economic rates. A lump sum today has certain value, while future royalty income does not, and that tradeoff is the real decision.

faqs.q: Can you sell your minerals if they're already under an existing lease?
faqs.a: Yes, you can sell the minerals subject to the existing lease, meaning the buyer steps into your position as the mineral and royalty owner going forward while the lease terms stay in place.

faqs.q: What if your acreage has never been leased at all?
faqs.a: You can still sell unleased minerals, though the value typically reflects the lack of current production history and depends more heavily on nearby drilling activity.

faqs.q: Does leasing mean drilling will definitely happen?
faqs.a: No. A lease gives the operator the right to drill during the lease term, but there's no guarantee a well gets drilled, especially on acreage outside the most active parts of the play.

faqs.q: Should you ask a CPA about the tax difference between leasing and selling?
faqs.a: Yes. Royalty income and proceeds from a mineral sale are generally treated differently for tax purposes, so it's worth discussing your specific situation with your CPA before making a decision.

faqs.q: What if a western North Dakota family disagrees about leasing versus selling?
faqs.a: This comes up often when several heirs share an interest. Splitting the acreage or selling only a portion while others keep theirs is a reasonable compromise if the family can't agree on one path for everyone.

items.name: Taxes When You Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: What to know about taxes before selling North Dakota mineral rights, including capital gains basics and why your CPA should see the deal early.

sections.html:
Selling mineral rights usually triggers a tax question the same week the offer arrives, and it's worth understanding the basics before that check lands in your account.

The North Dakota review specialists are not accountants, and the North Dakota review specialists won't pretend to be, but after selling minerals ourselves and talking with plenty of families who've done the same, the North Dakota review specialists have learned enough to know what questions to ask before closing. This isn't tax advice, it's a starting point so you walk into that conversation with your CPA informed instead of blindsided.

sections.title: The general shape of it
sections.html:
When you sell mineral rights, the proceeds are generally treated as the sale of a capital asset, meaning the gain, the difference between what you receive and your cost basis in the minerals, is typically subject to capital gains treatment rather than ordinary income tax rates. How long you held the interest can affect whether it's taxed at short-term or long-term rates, and inherited minerals often get a stepped-up basis based on their value at the time you inherited them.

This is different from royalty income, which is generally taxed as ordinary income each year as it's received. Selling the underlying minerals is a one-time event with its own tax treatment, separate from any royalty checks you may have received while you owned the interest.

sections.title: Why your cost basis matters
sections.html:
Your cost basis is essentially what the minerals were worth, for tax purposes, when you acquired them. If you inherited them, that's typically the fair market value at the time of the previous owner's death, not what your grandparents may have originally paid or been given the land for generations ago. If you purchased the minerals yourself, your basis is generally what you paid.

Establishing an accurate basis matters because it directly affects how much of the sale proceeds are treated as taxable gain. This is exactly the kind of detail your CPA can help pin down, especially for interests that have passed through more than one generation.

sections.title: Multiple heirs and shared ownership
sections.html:
When mineral interests are split among siblings or cousins, each owner's tax situation is generally handled separately based on their own share of the proceeds and their own basis in the interest. It's common for family members to assume the tax outcome will be identical for everyone, but differences in when each person inherited their share, or whether one heir bought out another's portion earlier, can change the picture for each individual.

This is worth discussing as a family before closing, so nobody is surprised by their portion of the tax outcome after the fact.

sections.title: Timing and why it's worth planning ahead
sections.html:
The tax year in which a sale closes matters, since it determines which year's return the transaction lands on. If you're weighing whether to close before or after year-end, or whether spreading a sale across more than one transaction makes sense for your situation, that's a conversation to have with your CPA before signing, not after the funds have already been wired.

None of this should scare you away from selling if it's the right decision for your family. It just means the tax side deserves the same attention as the offer itself.

When the North Dakota review specialists sold the review desk's own interest, the tax conversation with the review desk's CPA took less time than the North Dakota review specialists expected, mostly because the North Dakota review specialists brought the deed and estate paperwork with the review desk instead of showing up with just a number and a question.

faqs.q: Is selling mineral rights taxed the same as royalty income?
faqs.a: No. Royalty income is generally taxed as ordinary income as it's received, while proceeds from selling the underlying minerals are typically treated as a capital gain, which can be taxed differently depending on your basis and holding period.

faqs.q: What is cost basis and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Cost basis is generally what the minerals were worth for tax purposes when you acquired them, often the fair market value at the time of inheritance. It determines how much of your sale proceeds count as taxable gain.

faqs.q: Do you need to talk to a CPA before selling?
faqs.a: Yes, it's worth confirming your basis and expected tax treatment with your CPA or tax advisor before closing, especially for larger interests or those shared among multiple heirs.

faqs.q: Will each heir pay the same tax on a shared sale?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Each owner's basis and holding period can differ, so it's common for the tax outcome to vary between family members even on the same sale.

faqs.q: Does the timing of closing affect your taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, the tax year in which the sale closes determines which year's return it appears on, which is worth planning around with your CPA if you have flexibility on timing.

faqs.q: Are there any deductions you should ask your CPA about related to a mineral sale?
faqs.a: Depending on your situation, costs like legal or title fees connected to the sale may factor into the transaction, which is another reason to loop in your CPA before closing rather than after.

items.name: How Minerals Are Appraised
items.meta: How buyers actually value North Dakota mineral rights, from decline curve analysis to comparable sales, and why two offers can differ.

sections.html:
Two buyers can look at the same forty acres in McKenzie County and land on two different numbers, and understanding why helps you tell a careful offer from a lazy one.

When the North Dakota review specialists sold the review desk's own family's minerals, the first offer the North Dakota review specialists got felt like it was pulled out of thin air, a flat number with no explanation attached. The second buyer walked the review desk through how they got their number, well by well, and it was a completely different conversation. Appraisal isn't magic. It's a handful of methods, applied with more or less care depending on who's doing it.

sections.title: Production-based valuation
sections.html:
If your minerals are already producing, the most common approach is looking at the actual production history from the wells on your unit and projecting how that production is likely to decline going forward. Bakken and Three Forks wells tend to produce heavily in their first few years and then taper off along a decline curve, so a buyer is essentially estimating how many more years of royalty income that well is likely to generate and what that stream is worth today.

This means a well's age matters. A well that came online two years ago and is still near peak production values differently than one that's been declining for a decade, even if both are on similar-sized units with similar royalty terms.

sections.title: Valuing unleased or undeveloped acreage
sections.html:
If your minerals aren't leased or producing yet, there's no production history to project from, so buyers instead look at the acreage's position within the play, what nearby operators have been doing, and how recently similar tracts nearby have leased or sold. Acreage inside an active spacing unit with permits already filed carries different weight than acreage in a county that's seen little drilling activity in recent years.

This is also where offers vary the most, because it depends heavily on which nearby data points a buyer is willing to count and how they weigh the likelihood of future drilling.

sections.title: Comparable sales
sections.html:
Some buyers also look at what similar mineral interests nearby have recently sold for, the way a realtor might compare home sales in a neighborhood. This method has real limits in mineral valuation because two tracts a mile apart can sit in different spacing units with very different production, so a comparable sale is a data point, not the whole answer.

Be cautious of any offer that leans entirely on a comparable sale number without discussing the actual wells and production on your specific acreage. That's often a sign the buyer hasn't looked closely at what you actually own.

sections.title: Why value talk should always come with a range, not a promise
sections.html:
Oil prices move. Decline curves aren't perfectly predictable. Operators change drilling plans. Any honest number a buyer gives you is really a range tied to current activity and recent royalty checks, not a guarantee, and it's worth being skeptical of anyone who quotes a single number with total confidence before they've even seen your division orders.

A fair way to think about it is that your minerals are worth what a willing buyer will pay today, based on what's known right now about production and nearby drilling, and that number can shift as conditions shift.

The North Dakota review specialists have watched an offer on the same tract move meaningfully within a single year, once because a new well was permitted next door and once because oil prices pulled back. Neither change meant the earlier number was wrong, it just meant conditions had moved, which is the nature of valuing something tied to a commodity market and a decline curve rather than a fixed asset.

faqs.q: Do you need to pay for a formal appraisal before selling?
faqs.a: No. A serious buyer will evaluate your minerals as part of making an offer, using county records, division orders, and production data you provide, without requiring you to pay for a formal appraisal up front.

faqs.q: Why did you get such different offers from two buyers?
faqs.a: Buyers can weigh decline curves, future drilling potential, and comparable sales differently, which is normal. It's reasonable to ask each buyer to explain how they arrived at their number.

faqs.q: Does the type of well matter to value?
faqs.a: Yes. Newer horizontal wells in the Bakken or Three Forks typically have different production and decline patterns than older vertical wells, and that difference shows up in how a buyer projects future income.

faqs.q: What if there's no well on your acreage at all?
faqs.a: Unleased or undeveloped minerals can still have value, based mainly on the likelihood of future drilling given activity in nearby units, though that value is inherently less certain than producing acreage.

faqs.q: Can oil prices change what your minerals are worth?
faqs.a: Yes, royalty income and mineral values generally move with oil and gas prices, so an offer made today may differ from one made a year from now depending on market conditions.

faqs.q: Do buyers use software models or just estimate by hand?
faqs.a: Most serious buyers use some form of decline curve modeling for producing wells, combined with judgment about nearby drilling activity for undeveloped acreage. A careful buyer will still explain the reasoning in plain terms rather than hiding behind the model.

items.name: How Royalty Income Works

sections.title: Reconcile production to paid royalties
sections.html: For How Royalty Income Works, products, volumes, prices, taxes, deductions, paid decimals, downtime, and adjustments should reconcile to revenue actually received. Start with the owner statement rather than a basin-wide multiple. Match each payor line to the well, unit, product, sales month, decimal, and net amount, then compare that record with North Dakota production data and the controlling division order. Separate ordinary decline from shut-in time, workovers, corrected statements, and suspense releases. A useful income schedule explains why a check changed and identifies which missing record would confirm the explanation.

sections.title: Test one driver at a time
sections.html: Price, deductions, decline, downtime, development timing, title reserves, concentration, marketability, and discounting should be tested separately for How Royalty Income Works before scenarios are combined. Changing every input at once can make an attractive forecast impossible to audit. Hold the paid decimal and well list constant while testing commodity price, then hold price constant while testing decline or downtime. Keep existing producing wells apart from permits, offsets, and undeveloped inventory. The resulting range should show which assumption drives the outcome, which evidence supports it, and how quickly the conclusion changes when Bakken activity or owner records change.

sections.title: State the forecast horizon
sections.html: A How Royalty Income Works review distinguishes recent observed checks, medium-term decline, and longer-term development assumptions. Shut-in periods, workovers, recompletions, and terminal value remain visible. The first period should tie directly to statements and reported production. Later periods should identify the decline convention, price deck, deduction treatment, and date each assumption was observed. Possible future wells belong in a separate development schedule with operator, spacing, permit, offset, and timing evidence. That separation prevents uncommitted inventory from being presented as current income and gives the owner a clear path for updating the analysis after a new statement or regulatory filing arrives.

sections.title: Show the downside case
sections.html: The downside schedule for How Royalty Income Works can test lower prices, faster decline, longer downtime, higher deductions, delayed development, title-curative cost, and reduced marketability. It should not be a vague percentage haircut. Record the changed assumption, the reason for the change, and the line of the owner ledger it affects. For a concentrated North Dakota package, also test an operator delay, a single high-volume well going offline, and a title reserve that postpones payment. Comparing that case with the observed case helps an owner understand whether an offer reflects ordinary uncertainty or depends on an unusually pessimistic view of the property.

sections.title: Preserve the update path
sections.html: A How Royalty Income Works file is easier to refresh when it retains deeds, leases, division orders, statements, production records, operator notices, tax records, well lists, assumptions, and observation dates. Give every figure a source and every scenario an as-of date. Keep the legal-description schedule beside the well schedule so a later analyst can see which tracts and depths were included. Preserve unresolved questions instead of burying them inside a single value. When a new royalty statement, permit, order, or title document arrives, the owner should be able to replace one input and see the effect without rebuilding the entire property file from memory.

items.name: Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You?

sections.title: Put exchange planning before closing
sections.html: Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You? begins before the owner receives or controls proceeds. A potential exchanger should consult a qualified intermediary and independent tax counsel before closing. The working file should show the contemplated mineral sale, current vesting, expected proceeds, debt, closing date, and unresolved eligibility questions while there is still time to change the transaction sequence. Do not rely on a purchase offer or title conversation as tax guidance. The mineral evaluation can support property economics, but the intermediary and advisers must establish the exchange structure, permitted flow of funds, taxpayer consistency, and documents required before the relinquished interest closes.

sections.title: Write deadlines as calendar dates
sections.html: Identification and completion periods for Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You? should become actual dates beside intermediary instructions, property research, financing, title, backup choices, and closing tasks. Start the calendar from the actual relinquished-property closing rather than an estimated month. Record weekends and holidays without assuming they extend a federal deadline. Assign an owner to every task and keep backup replacement choices visible before identification. North Dakota mineral title work can consume time, so deeds, reservations, legal descriptions, and curative questions should enter the calendar early. A dated checklist is more useful than a summary that merely repeats the 45-day and 180-day numbers.

sections.title: Confirm taxpayer and vesting
sections.html: The Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You? file identifies the taxpayer, current vesting, relinquished interest, contract parties, proposed replacement property, debt, expected proceeds, and entity questions for qualified review. Compare the deed and contract names before signing, especially when minerals passed through an estate, trust, family entity, or marital transfer. List any proposed change in ownership separately and send it to the qualified intermediary and tax counsel rather than assuming it is harmless. The property schedule should also identify tracts, depths, products, retained interests, and exclusions so the advisers know exactly what is being sold and what replacement-property value and debt questions remain.

sections.title: Keep valuation and tax roles separate
sections.html: The Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You? owner ledger can compare property economics, but it does not determine eligibility, choose an identification rule, provide tax advice, act as intermediary, or direct closing funds. Use the ledger to compare documented income, title condition, concentration, development evidence, price assumptions, and marketability across candidate properties. Send eligibility, related-party, vesting, debt, boot, identification, and timing questions to the appropriate adviser. Keeping those roles distinct prevents a valuation conclusion from being mistaken for an exchange opinion and creates a cleaner record of who supplied each instruction before money or title moves.

sections.title: Archive the exchange evidence
sections.html: A completed Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You? file retains contracts, assignments, identification notices, delivery evidence, settlement statements, intermediary records, title documents, financing, value support, and adviser correspondence. Save the final signed versions, not only drafts or email summaries. Record when and how the identification notice was delivered and retain the accepted replacement-property description. Keep the mineral-property schedules and valuation assumptions that supported the decision at the time. That archive helps the owner, CPA, attorney, and intermediary reconstruct the transaction later without relying on memory, and it makes any post-closing correction or tax-reporting question easier to route to the right record.

Save the final signed versions, not only drafts or email summaries. Record when and how the identification notice was delivered and retain the accepted replacement-property description. Keep the mineral-property schedules and valuation assumptions that supported the decision at the time. That archive helps the owner, CPA, attorney, and intermediary reconstruct the transaction later without relying on memory, and it makes any post-closing correction or tax-reporting question easier to route to the right record.

items.name: Minerals as 1031 Replacement Property

sections.title: Put exchange planning before closing
sections.html: Minerals as 1031 Replacement Property begins before the owner receives or controls proceeds. A potential exchanger should consult a qualified intermediary and independent tax counsel before closing. The working file should show the contemplated mineral sale, current vesting, expected proceeds, debt, closing date, and unresolved eligibility questions while there is still time to change the transaction sequence. Do not rely on a purchase offer or title conversation as tax guidance. The mineral evaluation can support property economics, but the intermediary and advisers must establish the exchange structure, permitted flow of funds, taxpayer consistency, and documents required before the relinquished interest closes.

sections.title: Write deadlines as calendar dates
sections.html: Identification and completion periods for Minerals as 1031 Replacement Property should become actual dates beside intermediary instructions, property research, financing, title, backup choices, and closing tasks. Start the calendar from the actual relinquished-property closing rather than an estimated month. Record weekends and holidays without assuming they extend a federal deadline. Assign an owner to every task and keep backup replacement choices visible before identification. North Dakota mineral title work can consume time, so deeds, reservations, legal descriptions, and curative questions should enter the calendar early. A dated checklist is more useful than a summary that merely repeats the 45-day and 180-day numbers.

sections.title: Confirm taxpayer and vesting
sections.html: The Minerals as 1031 Replacement Property file identifies the taxpayer, current vesting, relinquished interest, contract parties, proposed replacement property, debt, expected proceeds, and entity questions for qualified review. Compare the deed and contract names before signing, especially when minerals passed through an estate, trust, family entity, or marital transfer. List any proposed change in ownership separately and send it to the qualified intermediary and tax counsel rather than assuming it is harmless. The property schedule should also identify tracts, depths, products, retained interests, and exclusions so the advisers know exactly what is being sold and what replacement-property value and debt questions remain.

sections.title: Keep valuation and tax roles separate
sections.html: The Minerals as 1031 Replacement Property owner ledger can compare property economics, but it does not determine eligibility, choose an identification rule, provide tax advice, act as intermediary, or direct closing funds. Use the ledger to compare documented income, title condition, concentration, development evidence, price assumptions, and marketability across candidate properties. Send eligibility, related-party, vesting, debt, boot, identification, and timing questions to the appropriate adviser. Keeping those roles distinct prevents a valuation conclusion from being mistaken for an exchange opinion and creates a cleaner record of who supplied each instruction before money or title moves.
